video_title: How Much Longer Can AI Carry the Market? ft. Christian Mueller-Glissmann | U Got Options | Ep.13
gist: Goldman's head of asset allocation research argues the market is in an AI earnings boom (not a valuation bubble) whose capex tailwind is peaking just as a fast bond selloff (10y ~5.3-5.4%) becomes the speed limit for equities; he sees equity and FX vol as cheap and favors diversification, gold and long-dated calls. The host adds a reflexive-liquidity, vol-suppression and imminent-debasement thesis.

themes.theme: AI capex boom: earnings bubble vs valuation bubble

insights.claim: The 2026 macro regime differs from year-start expectations: instead of a goldilocks inflation-relief setup, a huge AI capex boom re-accelerated the business cycle, releveraged a previously unlevered private sector and lifted nominal growth, while a Middle East war pushing energy prices drove most of the inflation.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann
insights.so_what: Nominal growth acceleration is good for equity earnings but bad for bonds, setting up the equity-bond tension.

insights.claim: The guest distinguishes an earnings bubble from a valuation bubble: he says markets are not in a valuation bubble but partly in an earnings bubble, which deflates slowly rather than bursting quickly.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann
insights.so_what: Argues for a grinding derating and dispersion rather than a tech-bubble-style crash, so risk management beats outright bearishness.
insights.quote: We are more likely to be a bit in an earnings bubble, at least in some of these parts of the market.

insights.claim: Valuations have already derated: the S&P 500 12-month forward PE fell from about 23x at the start of the year to about 19x, and the MSCI World forward PE is down roughly 15% year to date, showing the market is discounting cyclical AI earnings.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann
insights.so_what: Much skepticism is priced in, so a bad Q3 print is less of a surprise than headline Shiller multiples imply.

insights.claim: The Shiller PE (in the 40s, near tech-bubble levels) overstates stretch because the 10-year average lags a jump in profitability; S&P 500 ROE is around 24 versus below 20 five years ago and more than double late-1990s levels, so the question is how much of the profit step-up is structural.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann
insights.so_what: The bull-vs-bear valuation debate reduces to where corporate profitability settles over the next few years.

insights.claim: The host counters that earnings are about 50% above their long-run ~6% real trend and that past booms mean-revert beyond the mean for several years, with lower tax rates a one-time tailwind that populism could reverse into a headwind.
insights.speaker: Host
insights.so_what: Argues the profit-share gains are not a safe new structural plateau.

insights.claim: The AI capex tailwind to earnings is peaking, so the second derivative turns unfavorable; the next adoption/application phase is more uncertain, with a J-curve in which productivity gains are not yet visible in earnings or macro data, though the guest expects material productivity gains over the next decade.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann
insights.so_what: The market must shift from paying for capex-linked earnings to underwriting application revenue, increasing dispersion between winners and losers.

insights.claim: Hyperscaler free cash flow is negative and has diverged sharply from reported earnings while debt and CDS spreads rise; the host argues the earnings are not operational cash growth and that continuing growth requires more borrowing that crowds out the long end of the curve.
insights.speaker: Host
insights.so_what: Creates a circular debt-funded capex loop whose sustainability over years, not quarters, is doubtful.

insights.claim: Data center construction and compute contracts are unusually long-dated, giving more earnings visibility than a normal cycle; the guest says Goldman equity and strategy teams expect compute demand to stay high as use shifts from frontier-model development to applications.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann
insights.so_what: Explains why investors are not yet worried and why a near-term capex cliff is not the base case.

insights.claim: The Q3 earnings season is the key catalyst: hyperscalers must show AI monetization (cloud revenue) to justify negative FCF yields and future depreciation; otherwise valuations must fall further. The guest says a miss is not Goldman's baseline.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann
insights.so_what: A strong print lets equities digest higher yields; a weak one removes the growth source offsetting rate pressure.

insights.claim: Goldman's US strategy team finds S&P 500 companies spend only about 0.1% of cost of goods sold on AI tokens and subscriptions, implying large corporate adoption headroom but also that users are not paying fully for what they use.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann
insights.so_what: The monetization gap between AI usage and AI spend is the bridge the sector must cross.

themes.theme: Bonds as the equity speed limit

insights.claim: The 10-year Treasury yield at roughly 5.3-5.4% sits well above the 300-year average of about 4.7% (4.5% excluding the 1970s); the structural cycle, a fight between innovation and inflation, has become less friendly to long-duration bonds as AI investment crowds out bond demand, inflation volatility is higher and fiscal concerns grow.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann
insights.so_what: The market is still searching for a new equilibrium level for long yields, keeping pressure on duration.

insights.claim: The bond-equity interaction depends on level, speed and source: a 3-month rise in yields of more than two standard deviations typically brings indigestion, and the recent move to roughly 5.1-5.2% has exceeded that; and because the rise is driven by front-end real yields and policy rather than growth, it is less equity-friendly.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann
insights.so_what: Two of the three conditions (speed, source) currently argue against equities absorbing higher yields.

insights.claim: Damage from higher yields is visible underneath the index in small/mid caps, real estate, homebuilders and selective financials; the 5% threshold has been tolerated only because of the earnings tailwind in AI-linked parts of the market.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann
insights.so_what: If AI earnings momentum fades, the rate damage spreads from the periphery to the index.

insights.claim: Bond-market stress works with long lags because debt was financed near 0% in 2021 and average maturities are 5-8 years, so the refinancing wall is only now arriving, compounded by a simultaneous wave of new debt supply that outpaces demand despite Treasury buybacks, SLR changes and the stablecoin act.
insights.speaker: Host
insights.so_what: Rate pain is back-loaded; equity weakness from higher yields can arrive later than expected.

insights.claim: Central banks cannot easily step off the tightening pedal because they fear long-dated yields unanchoring; equity consolidation and higher volatility could stabilize bond yields and restore stock-bond diversification temporarily, though the guest does not expect 60/40 to return to its pre-COVID form.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann
insights.so_what: A short-term better equity-bond hedge is possible, but no structural return of the old 60/40 regime.

insights.claim: MOVE index and CDS are breaking out while the VIX remains quiet, a divergence between bond/credit stress and equity vol that the host flags as a signal.
insights.speaker: Host
insights.so_what: Equity vol looks underpriced relative to rates and credit risk.

themes.theme: Reflexivity, wealth effects and the market-economy loop

insights.claim: The host argues markets now drive the economy rather than reflect it: a roughly 20% equity rally in April-May added about $50 trillion of collateral/liquidity in two months versus $10 trillion of post-COVID QE, and this feeds capex, which feeds earnings, which feeds prices.
insights.speaker: Host
insights.so_what: The reflexive loop means a market decline would hit capex and earnings, making the system fragile and concentrated.

insights.claim: US household equity holdings as a share of wealth are at a record, above tech-bubble levels, and the spread versus residential real estate share is the widest ever, so a sharp equity correction would transmit strongly to the economy; the guest expects a Fed response to buffer it.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann
insights.so_what: The wealth-effect channel makes the economy more equity-dependent than ever, and policy support is the offset.

insights.claim: The guest cautions that comparisons with 1999 are imperfect: ROE is more than double 1990s levels and hyperscalers have diversified, profitable business models; the host replies that leverage flatters those return numbers.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann
insights.so_what: The bear analogy to 1999 is contested on profitability but agreed on concentration risk.

insights.claim: Equity volatility looks cheap versus credit spreads, rates vol and commodity vol; the guest leans toward upside convexity being cheap into year-end and favors slightly longer-dated calls, including on tech where single-stock vols reset after the summer momentum unwind.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann
insights.so_what: A cheap way to stay long the boom while keeping convex protection against a rates or AI shock.

insights.claim: Tech is compounding earnings at about 30% annualized, so a flat price means roughly 30% derating over a year; this makes large downside vol unlikely unless earnings growth's second derivative visibly rolls over, which is why vol is subdued.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann
insights.so_what: Downside vol is tied to an earnings-growth catalyst, so the earnings season is the vol trigger.

insights.claim: Nearly 40% of S&P 500 stocks had a negative beta to the index over the last 3 months and about 20-25% over the last year, which has not happened since the tech bubble; these are rate-sensitive, bond-proxy, low-vol and high-dividend names hurt by yields.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann
insights.so_what: The laggards are the natural diversifier if AI unwinds.

insights.claim: The host attributes the compressed index vol and record dispersion since 2017 to structured-product and systematic vol selling that pins the index; momentum flows and earnings revisions then amplify concentration into winners, which drives more capex. The guest says causality likely runs both ways since earnings dispersion is also near record.
insights.speaker: Host
insights.so_what: Index vol suppression and extreme dispersion are linked, and unpinning would produce violent reversals.

insights.claim: In the tech bust, the S&P 500 fell about 46% and the Nasdaq about 80%, while an S&P dividend aristocrats index or low-vol ETF rose about 10%; the guest cites this as evidence that defensive laggards diversify a concentrated equity book.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann
insights.so_what: Factor and sector diversification is the main portfolio tool against AI concentration.

insights.claim: Timing the peak of a boom is extremely hard (calling the bubble in 1998 meant being two years early), so the guest recommends preparing the portfolio via diversification, belly-of-the-curve bonds rather than long duration, factor diversification and equity volatility as an asset class rather than trying to time the top.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann
insights.so_what: Allocator value-add is only timing and diversification; prefer the latter now.
insights.quote: there's always two value ads that you have as an asset allocator market timing and diversification.

insights.claim: The host says in the 1998-2000 bubble the best trade was owning out-of-the-money calls or cheap long-dated vol rather than stocks, and expects bubble markets to move in megaphone patterns.
insights.speaker: Host
insights.so_what: Long convexity is a way to participate in a late-stage boom without shorting it.

insights.claim: FX volatility is also remarkably cheap given recent violent moves in the yen, euro and Swiss franc; FX vol expressions could become valuable for protecting non-home-currency assets.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann
insights.so_what: Currency convexity is a second cheap hedge as policy shifts raise FX risk.

insights.claim: Timing geopolitical shocks is not feasible, so asset allocators emphasize robustness: real assets that cushion policy-induced inflation, gold as convexity on loss of trust, and more attention to FX risk.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann
insights.so_what: Portfolio construction rather than prediction is the response to political volatility.

insights.claim: Global asset owners are showing more home bias because of FX risk from large policy shifts, seen first in bonds and increasingly in equities.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann
insights.so_what: Reduces foreign demand for US assets at the margin and favors currency-matched allocation.

insights.claim: Bonds are becoming a less reliable equity hedge worldwide because of fiscal concerns and political volatility, whereas in a low-inflation fiscal-austerity world they were a good buffer; this changes what investors can do with duration.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann
insights.so_what: Hedging needs to shift toward gold, vol and real assets rather than long bonds.

insights.claim: Gold offers convexity to trust problems: it rallied on distrust of central banks in the 1970s, of the financial system in the GFC and of governments since COVID, and Goldman remains constructive on gold as a diversifier.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann
insights.so_what: Gold is the preferred hedge against policy and trust risk.

insights.claim: The host predicts US debasement will arrive within the next year, not in 5-10 years, and will be a highly convex event for global markets, an earthquake though not necessarily a market decline.
insights.speaker: Host
insights.so_what: Positioning should assume currency debasement rather than depend on a benign debt resolution.

insights.claim: The host expects the next downturn to be met with massive QE plus a cap on the long end of the curve, creating a structural inflation loop, followed by direct state investment (sovereign wealth fund, Trump accounts) into equities and corporations in a China/Japan-style model, since the market is too big to fail.
insights.speaker: Host
insights.so_what: State backstops could extend the capex boom but at the cost of inflation and currency debasement.

insights.claim: The host recommends holding the same positions as the government: gold, farmland and leverage on real estate, arguing that being under-levered may be the greatest risk in a debasement.
insights.speaker: Host
insights.so_what: Real-asset ownership financed with fixed-rate debt benefits from debasement.

insights.claim: A host study of the 1960s-70s found FX, bond and gold volatility dramatically outperformed any other period while industrial commodities and equities underperformed, with equities going nowhere in nominal terms from 1968 to 1982 as margin compression and rising discount rates offset nominal growth.
insights.speaker: Host
insights.so_what: A debasement/inflation regime may favor vol and currency-like assets over equity beta.
